rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.7, 3.2, Table 2 <U+2014> authors developed a float-sensor/RF/microcontroller automated irrigation system and field-tested it at ICAR-CIAE Bhopal in Kharif 2018-19 on rice (PUSA 1121), measuring pump discharge with a water meter and recording yield and growth. Q2: Section 3.2 and Table 2 <U+2014> the automated (AWD) system achieved 36% total water savings versus the continuous-ponding control, with irrigation water productivity 6.15 vs 3.06 kg/ha/mm; this falls within the review's 11-42% range for sensor-microcontroller-actuation smart irrigation. Q7: Discussion (p. 4734-4735) and Section 2.6 <U+2014> authors state the system requires a reliable power source, the pump house must lie within the 100 m RF communication range of the field sensor, the field must be laser-levelled before installation for smooth water flow, and farmers may need special training to operate and maintain it. Q8: Conclusions and Discussion <U+2014> authors state the study primarily compares AWD with continuous ponding and focuses on system development and water saving rather than the system's specific effect on crop performance; prototype limited to 100 m range, larger fields would need multiple sensors/valves, single season and single plot comparison.
rows.notes: Water saving measured only by a mechanical water meter (one method), single site, single season, two plots. The 36% saving is confounded: the control was continuous ponding, so the saving reflects AWD scheduling rather than automation per se (authors acknowledge this in the Conclusions); the automated system is nonetheless the sensor-microcontroller-actuation 'smart irrigation' the review defines, so Q2 is accepted. No intermediate variable (percolation, seepage, number of irrigation events, water-level time series) reported for Q4. Standard deviation is given only for yield (4.8<U+00B1>0.189 vs 4.1/4.2<U+00B1>0.429 t/ha), not for the water saving or water productivity, so Q9 is no. Note minor inconsistency in control yield (4.2 in text vs 4.1 in Table 2). No 'app' involved; technology is a microcontroller/RF system rather than an app, but it matches the review's definition of smart irrigation.

notes: Full text available; some pages contain duplicated OCR lines from a peer-review overlay but content is complete. Study is a single-season, single-plot prototype test comparing automated AWD against continuous flooding.
